title: Part III — SUPPLY: Getting Inventory In
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published page (posts/part-3-intro/index.md) and its former spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces; one spec paragraph per unit of the page, in the page's order. Intent outcome, AC-1 to AC-3 and role are copied unchanged from the post's entry in journal-spec.json; the introduction realises Part III's opening (hook, bridge, roadmap) from the same file. The journal spec gives this post no thesis, so the thesis and its three supporting claims are written here from the part's thesis and flow. The five callouts (IN THIS PART, WHY THE BUSINESS CARES, WHY ARCHITECTS SHOULD CARE, KEY POINTS, FAILURE PATTERNS) stand before the first paragraph and are kept as the house format; the KEY POINTS callout carries the part's claim in three bullets. thesis.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?
thesis.claim: Part III argues that supply is one chain, not five features: every door writes through one path under its own contract, every value keeps its original and its recorded source, listings of the same thing are recognized as one, and publication is a decision followed by a propagation whose removal side matters more; its five chapters take the links in the order a record meets them and end with professional tooling, where the professionals who supply most of the inventory check the chain's output against their own systems.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of treating each door, the deduplication job, the index and the pro dashboard as separate features owned by the teams that built them, so the supply chapters are a set of independent topics a reader may consult in any order.
thesis.so_what: A reader who accepts it reads ingestion first, or opens the one chapter that answers the supply problem in front of them, and expects every later part (search, alerts, recommendations) to inherit whatever weakness a link of the chain leaves.
thesis.how_why: Normalization works only on records ingestion accepted; entity resolution compares the canonical values normalization produces; the publication pipeline budgets stages the reader has by then met; and professional tooling reconciles leads from listings already published, which is why it comes last. Veldmark meets each link first as an incident: a truncated file that unpublished 38,400 Motorvane listings, a six-minute baseline that ignored held listings, 23 portal leads against 14 in a dealer's CRM.

supporting_claims.claim: The five chapters take the chain's links in the order a record meets them, and each is the chapter to open first for a recognizable symptom.
The chain sits between the book's other parts: it consumes Part II's contracts, takes its targets from Part I's liquidity metrics and delivers what Part IV reads.
Veldmark meets each link first as an incident or a mismatch and answers it with a contract or a design, one per chapter.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states that supply is one chain with a contract, a provenance record and a removal path at every link, the reading order of the five chapters and the Veldmark incidents they answer.

flow.rationale: The page opens on the problem (supply arriving through many doors, each growing its own idea of a listing), states the part's claim (one chain) together with the order in which the chapters take its links, then narrows to one row per chapter with the symptom that sends a reader there. It then widens once to place the chain in the book, shows Veldmark meeting each link as an incident in chapter order, and ends with a short synthesis that hands off to the first chapter. The professionals' check is stated as the chain's last link, where its output is checked, so that 'five features' and five chapters agree. The order of the chapters is stated before the table because the rows only make sense once the reader knows they follow one record; the connection section follows the table because it says what the chapters take from Parts I and II; the Veldmark section follows the connection because its incidents are the chain's weaknesses in practice, listed in chapter order; the conclusion comes last, holds no new material and carries the forward link to Part IV, which is the chain's so-what. Put Veldmark first and the incidents arrive before the reader knows which link each belongs to; put the connection first and it names contracts and targets before the reader knows which chapters use them.
